answer: When a brand-new user logs in for the first time via Google, two external notifications are triggered after the user record is created: (1) Power Automate webhook (power_automate_client.trigger_new_user_registration): Sends an HTTP POST to the configured POWER_AUTOMATE_NEW_USER_WEBHOOK_URL with payload {user_email, user_name, login_provider}. Called in get_or_create_user() in utils/auth.py after session.commit() and session.refresh(new_user). If it fails, the exception is caught and logged as a warning — user creation is NOT rolled back. If the webhook URL is not configured (new_user_enabled=False), it returns False and logs a warning. (2) Novu subscriber sync (novu_service.create_or_update_subscriber): Called in main.py's /verify endpoint after get_or_create_user() returns. Creates/updates a Novu subscriber with subscriber_id=user.id, email=user.email, first_name=user.display_name. If this fails, the exception is caught and logged as a warning — does NOT affect the login flow. Both notifications are non-blocking: failures are caught, logged, and silently ignored. The user login succeeds regardless.

The system uses email as the primary identifier for cross-provider account linking. In get_or_create_user() (utils/auth.py), the first lookup is select(User).where(User.email == email). When the same email logs in first via Google then via Facebook: After Google login (new user created): email is set, entra_sub_google = Google's entra sub value, entra_sub_facebook = NULL, last_login_provider = 'google.com', display_name = name from Google JWT, roles = ['user']. After Facebook login (existing user found by email): entra_sub_facebook is SET to the new Facebook entra sub value (via setattr(user, field_name, entra_sub) using IDP_FIELD_MAPPING {'google.com': 'entra_sub_google', 'facebook.com': 'entra_sub_facebook', ...}), last_login_provider is UPDATED to 'facebook.com', last_login_at is UPDATED, updated_at is UPDATED. display_name is NOT overwritten because the condition 'not user.display_name' is False (already set from Google login). entra_sub_google remains unchanged.

Complete data flow for /verify with valid JWT NOT in cache: (1) Token extraction from Authorization: Bearer <token> header, or fallback to session cookie. (2) Redis cache check via jwt_cache.get(token): generates key as 'jwt_cache:' + hashlib.sha256(token.encode()).hexdigest()[:16], Redis GET returns None (cache miss), metrics.misses += 1. (3) Entra JWT verification via verify_entra_jwt(token): fetches JWKS from https://{ENTRA_TENANT_ID}.ciamlogin.com/{ENTRA_TENANT_ID}/discovery/v2.0/keys, finds matching RSA public key by kid from JWT header, verifies RS256 signature, audience (ENTRA_CLIENT_ID), and issuer. Returns decoded JWT payload dict. (4) User lookup/creation via get_or_create_user(entra_payload): determines IDP from payload's 'idp' claim (fallback to 'iss'), queries PostgreSQL SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = <email>. If exists: links IDP sub field, updates last_login_provider, last_login_at, updated_at. If new: creates record with roles=['user'], triggers Power Automate webhook. (5) Novu subscriber sync via novu_service.create_or_update_subscriber. (6) Redis cache set via jwt_cache.set(token, user_data): stores JSON with TTL 780 seconds (13 minutes). Stored data: {user_id, email, display_name, roles, entra_sub, idp, cached_at}. (7) Response: HTTP 200 with body 'OK' and headers x-user-id (UUID), x-email (email), x-roles (comma-separated roles). Systems touched: Redis → Entra JWKS endpoint (HTTP) → PostgreSQL → Power Automate (if new user) → Novu API → Redis (write back).

To add a new updatable field 'address' to user profile (read + write), ALL required changes: (1) app/models/user.py — add DB column: address = Column(Text). (2) Database migration — Alembic migration or ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN address TEXT. (3) app/models/user_schemas.py — add to UserProfileResponse: address: Optional[str]; add to UserProfileUpdateRequest: address: Optional[str] = Field(None, max_length=200). Update json_schema_extra examples. (4) app/api/user.py — update get_user_profile endpoint: add address=user.address to UserProfileResponse() constructor. (5) The PUT endpoint needs NO code change — it already uses a generic loop: for field, value in update_dict.items(): if hasattr(user, field): setattr(user, field, value). Since 'address' would be in UserProfileUpdateRequest and User model has the column, it's automatically handled. Summary: 3 files changed + 1 DB migration.

POST /profile/picture (direct upload): Receives an UploadFile directly. Calls blob_manager.upload_to_permanent(file, 'users', user_id) — uploads directly to the permanent 'users' container in Azure Blob Storage, no temp staging. Validates image format, size ≤10MB, dimensions ≤2048x2048 via PIL. Generates blob name: {user_id}_{timestamp}_{md5_hash[:8]}.{ext}. After upload, verifies blob properties. Updates user.profile_picture_url in DB, then calls cleanup_old_images([old_url]). PUT /profile (inline update): Receives profile_picture_url as a string URL. Three sub-paths: (a) URL contains 'temp-uploads/': calls move_blob_image() which copies from temp-uploads to users container (server-side copy via start_copy_from_url, polls up to 30s), then deletes temp blob. (b) URL is None (delete): calls cleanup_old_images([old_url]). (c) URL is already permanent: just updates DB. Cleanup strategy: Old permanent images are NOT directly deleted. cleanup_old_images() calls move_to_temp(url) which copies blob from permanent container to temp-uploads, then deletes from permanent. The temp-uploads container has a 24-hour Azure lifecycle policy that auto-deletes blobs. This provides a safety window for accidental deletions.

User profile API endpoints (/api/v1/users/*) use Depends(get_current_user) from utils/dependencies.py: extracts user info from Nginx-forwarded HTTP headers (x-user-id, x-email, x-roles) declared as Header(...) FastAPI dependencies. Validates UUID format, email contains @ and ., roles are non-empty. Returns {user_id, email, roles} dict. No JWT handling — trusts Nginx's pre-validation. The /verify endpoint in main.py directly handles JWT validation itself: extracts raw token from Authorization: Bearer header or session cookie, checks Redis cache for cached user data, on miss calls verify_entra_jwt(token) which validates against Microsoft Entra JWKS (fetches public keys, verifies RS256 signature, audience, issuer), then calls get_or_create_user() to query/create in PostgreSQL. Returns user info as response headers (x-user-id, x-email, x-roles) which Nginx forwards to downstream services. Key difference: /verify does cryptographic JWT validation + DB lookup; profile endpoints rely on Nginx having already called /verify and just read forwarded headers. Two-tier architecture.

If a LINE account is already bound to a different user: In link_line() (api/user.py), after obtaining LINE user ID, it queries select(User).where(User.line_user_id == line_user_id). If found AND str(existing_user.id) != current_user['user_id'], it raises HTTP 409 Conflict with detail '此 LINE 帳號已被其他使用者綁定'. The linking is rejected. If the same user re-links, it proceeds normally. Database fields affected when LINKING: line_user_id = LINE userId, line_display_name = LINE displayName, line_picture_url = LINE pictureUrl, line_linked_at = datetime.utcnow(). Database fields affected when UNLINKING: line_user_id = NULL, line_display_name = NULL, line_picture_url = NULL, line_linked_at = NULL. All four fields on users table. line_user_id has unique=True constraint ensuring one LINE account per user.

In core/database.py, the async engine uses postgresql+asyncpg:// driver for FastAPI async endpoints, while the sync engine replaces the URL scheme: sync_database_url = settings.DATABASE_URL.replace('postgresql+asyncpg://', 'postgresql://') to use the standard psycopg2 driver. Both exist because: (1) FastAPI's async endpoints need async DB sessions (AsyncSessionFactory with AsyncSession) for non-blocking I/O; (2) Some code requires synchronous DB access — the sync session factory (SyncSessionFactory via sessionmaker bound to sync_engine) is described as 'for vendor API' and provides the get_db() dependency yielding sync Session objects. The Novu SDK calls are also synchronous. If you removed the sync session factory: any endpoint or service using Depends(get_db) — which returns a sync Session — would break. The get_db() generator function uses SyncSessionFactory directly. All code relying on synchronous SQLAlchemy sessions would fail with no session factory available.

Cache key generation: JWTCache._get_cache_key(token) computes hashlib.sha256(token.encode()).hexdigest()[:16] and prepends 'jwt_cache:' — resulting in 'jwt_cache:{first 16 chars of SHA-256 hex}'. Data stored: JSON-serialized dict containing {user_id, email, display_name, roles, entra_sub, idp, cached_at}. TTL: settings.JWT_CACHE_TTL = 780 seconds (13 minutes). Redis unavailability handling: In get(), if Redis connection fails or any exception occurs during redis_client.get(), the exception is caught, metrics.errors is incremented, a warning is logged, and None is returned — causing a cache miss. The system then proceeds to full Entra JWT verification + PostgreSQL lookup (the normal non-cached path). In set(), if Redis fails during setex(), the exception is similarly caught and logged as warning — the verified result simply isn't cached. In _get_redis(), if the initial ping fails, it tries to rebuild the connection; if that also fails, the exception propagates up to get()/set() where it's caught. The system gracefully degrades to no-cache mode when Redis is completely unavailable.

Existing infrastructure to reuse: (1) utils/dependencies.py provides get_current_user() which extracts {user_id, email, roles} from Nginx headers (x-user-id, x-email, x-roles). (2) require_vendor_role() and require_admin_role() are existing role guard patterns — Depends on get_current_user then checks if the required role is in current_user['roles']. (3) A generic factory require_role(required_role: str) returns a dependency function checking for any role name. For a 'designer' role endpoint, you'd use Depends(require_role('designer')). Role data flow: (a) User logs in → /verify validates JWT → get_or_create_user() reads user.roles from PostgreSQL (JSON array column, e.g. ['user', 'designer']). (b) /verify returns x-roles header with comma-separated roles (e.g. 'user,designer'). (c) Nginx forwards x-roles to downstream services. (d) Downstream endpoint uses Depends(get_current_user) which parses x-roles header into a list. (e) Role guard checks if 'designer' is in current_user['roles'], raises HTTP 403 if not.

The three possible target tables are: (1) brands — when brand_type is 'material', (2) equipment_brands — when brand_type is 'kitchen_equipment' or 'bathroom_equipment', and (3) decoration_brands — when brand_type is 'decoration'. The routing is controlled by the brand_type input value (a Literal type accepting 'material', 'kitchen_equipment', 'bathroom_equipment', or 'decoration'). This logic is implemented in the _create_brand() function in catalog_submission.py.

The system uses a generation-based cache invalidation mechanism. When a new product is created (or updated/deleted), invalidate_product_cache() is called, which increments a Redis generation counter key ({prefix}products:cache:gen) using r.incr(). All search cache keys include the generation number (format: {prefix}products:search:v{gen}:{param_hash}), built by build_search_cache_key(). When the generation increments, all existing search cache keys become orphaned (they reference the old generation number and will never match new lookups), effectively invalidating all search caches without needing to delete them individually. The orphaned keys expire naturally via their TTL (SEARCH_CACHE_TTL = 120 seconds). For product detail cache, if a product_id is provided, it also directly deletes the specific detail cache key.

The export endpoint (export_materials_list in favorites.py) builds the category string using the _build_category_from_joined_data() helper function, which takes pre-joined data from AreaProduct, PaintProduct, KitchenEquipment, BathroomEquipment, and DecorationProduct. The category string is constructed by joining parts with ' - ' separator (e.g., ['材料', material_type, material_subtype] → '材料 - 石材 - 水磨石'). No additional database queries are needed because the main export query already performs LEFT JOINs on all five product type tables along with FavoriteItem, Product, ProductImage, Brand, and Vendor — all in a single query. The category/subcategory fields (material_type, material_subtype, equipment_category, decoration_category) are already available from the joined result tuples.

When updating images, the system performs smart image management in the update_product endpoint: (1) Extract UUIDs from all current images (primary + other_images) using _extract_uuid_from_image_object(), which gets UUID from 'uuid' field or by parsing filename from the 'original' URL. (2) Extract UUIDs from all new images. (3) Compute set difference to find removed UUIDs (current_all_uuids - new_all_uuids). (4) For each removed UUID, call blob_client.move_image_group_to_temp_for_cleanup() to move all size variants (original, medium, thumbnail) to a temp folder for later cleanup. (5) For new uploads (images with 'uuid' field from staging area), process via blob_client.move_multi_size_images() in batch to move from staging to permanent products folder. (6) Existing kept images (no 'uuid' field, already have 'original' URL) are passed through as-is. (7) The final list preserves the frontend's ordering. DB record updated with flag_modified(images, 'other_images') to ensure SQLAlchemy detects JSONB change.

The constraint is enforced in the create_collection endpoint in favorites.py. When data.is_public is False, the system queries existing private collections with FavoriteCollection.is_public == False using with_for_update() (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) which acquires row-level locks. If len(private_collections) >= 3, it raises HTTP 400 'Maximum 3 private collections allowed'. The with_for_update() lock prevents race conditions: two concurrent requests to create private collections will have the second block on the row lock until the first commits, then correctly see the updated count. The same pattern is also used in update_collection when changing from public to private — it locks other private collections (excluding the current one) and checks count >= 3.

The system uses a two-level sorting strategy with a CASE WHEN priority expression. In the DB query, priority_expr = case((price_field < 1, 1), else_=0). Products with price < 1 (including zero) get priority=1, normal-priced products get priority=0. ORDER BY sorts by priority ASC first (priority=0 before 1), then actual price, then composite_score as tiebreaker. This pushes zero/low-price products to the bottom. When merging results from area_products and paint_products, merge_sorted_product_lists() uses get_comparable_price() returning a (priority, price) tuple where priority=1 for prices < 1. The merge uses an O(n) merge-sort algorithm to combine pre-sorted lists.

The three phases in catalog upload endpoints (upload_catalog, upload_equipment_catalog, upload_decoration_catalog in catalogs.py): Phase 1: Quick DB validation — opens SessionLocal(), performs fast validation (verify brand exists, vendor exists, check duplicates), extracts needed IDs, then closes with db.close() in finally block. Phase 2: HTTP uploads (no DB connection held) — performs slow operations: streaming file upload to Azure Blob Storage and optional cover image upload. No database connection held. Phase 3: Quick DB write — opens fresh SessionLocal(), creates catalog record, commits, closes. This pattern is necessary because catalog uploads involve streaming large files (up to 100MB for material catalogs, 50MB for equipment/decoration) to external blob storage, which can take significant time. Holding a DB connection during slow HTTP upload would exhaust the connection pool under load.

The catalog hashtag update is queued by queue_catalog_hashtag_update() in products.py. Trigger: called after a product is created (create_product), updated (update_product), or deleted (delete_product). Data structure: inserts into catalog_hashtag_queue table via raw SQL: INSERT INTO catalog_hashtag_queue (catalog_id, catalog_type) VALUES (:catalog_id, :catalog_type) ON CONFLICT (catalog_id, catalog_type) DO NOTHING. The ON CONFLICT ensures idempotency. Catalog type determination: for area_product or paint_product → catalog_type='material' using product_data.catalog_id; for kitchen_equipment or bathroom_equipment → catalog_type='equipment' using equipment_catalog_id; for decoration → catalog_type='decoration' using decoration_catalog_id. Queued entries are later processed by a cron job.

The _get_catalogs_with_products() function uses an optimized batch query approach: Step 1 (Material): fetches all material catalog IDs, then executes a CTE (ranked_products) with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.catalog_id ORDER BY p.id) to get max 6 products per catalog. Tables: products, product_images, area_products, paint_products (LEFT JOIN). Step 2 (Equipment): fetches all equipment catalog IDs, runs two batch queries — one for kitchen_equipment (max 3 via CTE) and one for bathroom_equipment (max 3), both joining products and product_images. Results merged per catalog with total cap of 6. Step 3 (Decoration): batch query joining decoration_products, products, product_images with ROW_NUMBER limited to 6. Tables across all three domains: Material: catalogs, products, product_images, area_products, paint_products; Equipment: equipment_catalogs, products, product_images, kitchen_equipment, bathroom_equipment; Decoration: decoration_catalogs, products, product_images, decoration_products. This avoids N+1 queries by using window functions.

Given product ID 50 in catalog [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70] with limit=5: Step 1 (after_query): query products with ID > 50, ORDER BY ID ASC, LIMIT 5 → [60, 70] (2 products). Step 2 (before_query): needed = 5 - 2 = 3, query products with ID < 50, ORDER BY ID ASC, LIMIT 3 → [10, 20, 30]. Step 3 (merge): after_query + before_query = [60, 70, 10, 20, 30]. Returned IDs: [60, 70, 10, 20, 30] — first products after the current one, then wrapping to the beginning. If there's no catalog_id: the function falls back to using subcategory parameter (e.g., material_subtype for area_product, paint_type for paint_product). If neither catalog_id nor subcategory is provided, returns an empty list with source='none'.

When a new vendor registers through POST /vendors/me, two external integrations are triggered: (1) Power Automate notification via power_automate_client.trigger_vendor_application(), sending company_name, contact_person, phone, address, company_email, tax_id, line_id. (2) EasyAppointments provider creation via ea_client.create_provider() (only if settings.EA_API_KEY is configured), creating a provider with a randomly generated password (secrets.token_urlsafe(12)) and storing ea_provider_id on the vendor record. Both are non-blocking — if Power Automate fails, a warning is logged but request succeeds. If EA provider creation fails, warning is logged and vendor just won't have ea_provider_id. Neither failure causes rollback.

The Gallery API (GET /api/v1/gallery/portfolios) merges DesignerPortfolio and CrewPortfolio. Cover image extraction differs: For designers, uses DesignerPortfolio.cover_image_url (dedicated URL field), falling back to picsum.photos placeholder if null. For crews, uses CrewPortfolio.images (JSONB array) + cover_image_index — accesses images[cover_image_index], if element is dict with 'url' key extracts URL, if plain string uses directly, falls back to placeholder. Budget unit conversion: budget_min/budget_max are stored in 萬元 (10,000 NTD) in DB, the Gallery API converts to 元 (NTD) by multiplying by 10,000. Filter parameters come in as 元, so API divides by 10,000 (// 10000) when querying.

The five scoring dimensions and weights are: (1) location (地理位置): 0.30 — uses Haversine distance between city coordinates; (2) specialty (專業技能): 0.25 — compares required vs crew specialties using set intersection ratio; (3) budget (預算匹配): 0.20 — calculates overlap between project and crew budget ranges; (4) availability (可用性): 0.15 — checks availability_status and team_size for capacity; (5) history (歷史績效): 0.10 — queries the external crew_performance_history table for total_projects_completed, average_rating, on_time_completion_rate, and customer_satisfaction_score. The history dimension is the one querying an external table (not crews).

To add 'rating_avg' to the public crew list API response: (1) app/models/schemas.py — add rating_avg field to CrewListItem Pydantic model; (2) app/api/crews.py — modify _build_crew_list_item() helper to include rating_avg, and modify list_crews() to query CrewReview for average ratings; (3) Optionally app/models/database.py if adding a denormalized column. Authentication pattern: header-based via get_current_user() dependency extracting x-user-id, x-email, x-roles from Nginx-forwarded headers. Public endpoints like GET /crews don't require authentication (no Depends), authenticated endpoints use Depends(get_current_user).

The crew list endpoint uses a REGION_TO_CITIES dictionary. For service_area='北部地區', it maps to ['台北市', '新北市', '桃園市', '基隆市', '新竹市', '新竹縣', '宜蘭縣']. It creates OR filters: for each city, Crew.service_areas.contains([city]), combined with or_(*city_filters). This matches any crew whose service_areas JSONB array contains at least one city in the region. Special case: '全台服務' maps to None (no filter, all crews match). If the value is a direct city name (not in REGION_TO_CITIES), it falls to else branch: direct filter Crew.service_areas.contains([service_area]) checking for that exact city.

For vendor deletion (DELETE /vendors/me): Beyond database deletion, two cleanup operations: (1) Blob storage cleanup — if vendor has logo_url, calls blob_client.delete_vendor_logo() to remove logo from Azure Blob Storage (failure logged as warning, doesn't block). (2) EasyAppointments provider deletion — if vendor has ea_provider_id and EA_API_KEY configured, calls ea_client.delete_provider() (failure logged as warning). Role system update: handled via PostgreSQL database trigger — when vendor record is deleted, the trigger automatically removes the 'vendor' role from the user. For designer deletion: associated DesignerPortfolio records deleted first (foreign key), then designer profile; role changes rely on PostgreSQL triggers.

The three database models are: (1) SOPTemplate (sop_templates) — top-level template with specialty (工種), name, description, steps (JSONB array of check steps), created_by (FK to designers.id). One-to-many with SOPChecklist. (2) SOPChecklist (sop_checklists) — project-level execution instance, linked to SOPTemplate via template_id (FK), project_id, crew_id (FK to crews). Contains status (pending/in_progress/completed/failed), started_at, completed_at, notes. (3) SOPViolation (sop_violations) — violation records linked via checklist_id (FK). Tracks step_id, violation_type (skip/delay/quality_issue/safety), severity (low/medium/high/critical), description, resolution. Step completion tracking: uses completed_steps JSONB field on SOPChecklist. POST /checklists/{id}/complete-step uses step_id as key in the JSONB dict, value is {completed_at, notes, photos, crew_member}. First step completion sets started_at and status to 'in_progress'.

Material linkage is stored in DesignerPortfolio.linked_materials JSONB field as array of objects: [{"product_id": 540, "usage_area": "廚房"}] (max 10 per portfolio). Product details are fetched by extracting all product_ids, then querying Product table LEFT JOINed with ProductImage (on ProductImage.product_id == Product.id) filtered by Product.id.in_(product_ids). Results assembled into product_map keyed by product.id with product_id, product_name, product_image. Image resolution priority: from ProductImage.primary_image JSONB, first tries 'medium', falls back to 'original' (image.primary_image.get('medium') or image.primary_image.get('original')). Final materials list merges product details with usage_area.

When an activity is added to a CRM contact (POST /contacts/{contact_id}/activities), two side effects on the contact record: (1) contact.last_contact_at updated to datetime.now(timezone.utc); (2) contact.updated_at updated to current UTC timestamp. The activity records bd_user_id from the authenticated user. Role-based access control for team performance: GET /bd-performance/team checks if current user has any of: 'admin', 'director', 'team_lead', 'bd_manager'. Missing all → HTTP 403 'Insufficient permissions'. Individual BD performance (GET /bd-performance) only requires basic authentication.

Two pricing tiers: (1) 'monthly' — NT$3,000 (300,000 cents), 30 days; (2) 'yearly' — NT$30,000 (3,000,000 cents), 365 days. Expiration calculation on re-subscribe: if designer.premium_expires_at exists and is in the future (> now), new expiration extends from current expiry: expires_at = designer.premium_expires_at + duration. If expired or not set, calculated from now. However, there's a guard raising HTTP 409 if already active Premium subscriber, so the extension logic applies only if is_premium is False but premium_expires_at is still future (edge case). Payment transaction recorded via _record_premium_transaction() function, currently a stub (pass). Docstring indicates it would call interaction-service POST /api/v1/payments/ with amount, payer/payee, payment_method 'newebpay', transaction_type 'payment'. Transaction ID: 'PREM-{uuid4 hex[:12] uppercase}'. Recording failure is caught and ignored.

The downstream operation is write_through_material() in rfq_chat_helpers.py. When a homeowner confirms a quote, each confirmed quote item triggers write_through_material(), which upserts into rfq_project_materials table. If existing material found (matched by source_quote_item_id or name within same chat_room), it updates: status → 'confirmed', quoted_price (= item.subtotal), quantity, unit, quoted_responder_id, quoted_responder_name, quoted_responder_logo_url, syncs thumbnail ↔ image_url bidirectionally, material_type (mapped from item_type: 'labor'→'labor_only', 'material'→'material'). If no existing material found, creates new RfqProjectMaterial with: project_id, name, quantity, unit, status='confirmed', quoted_price, quoted_responder_id, quoted_responder_name, quoted_responder_logo_url, chat_room_id, from_requirement_id (from RfqRequirementResponder lookup), material_type, source_quote_item_id, thumbnail (from item.image_url).

notify_new_chat_message() in rfq_notification_service.py triggers the notification flow, called from rfq_chat_messages.py after a text message is committed. It calls _send_all() dispatching to four channels: (1) In-app notification: writes RfqNotification record with type='chat_message'. (2) Novu (email + in-app bell): triggers workflow 'quote-response-received' via novu_service_simple. (3) Web Push: calls web_push_service.send_to_user() which checks NotificationPreference — if push_enabled is False or specific type preference disabled, returns 0 and skips. If no active PushSubscription records exist, also skips. (4) LINE push: calls get_line_user_id() looking up users.line_user_id — if user has no line_user_id (not bound to LINE), returns None and LINE push is skipped.

Two authentication mechanisms: (1) get_current_user from app.utils.dependencies — extracts identity from Nginx-forwarded HTTP headers (x-user-id, x-email, x-roles). Returns dict {user_id, email, roles}. Used by most API endpoints: rfq_chat_messages, rfq_chat_quotes, rfq_chat_rooms, rfq_upload, rfq_notifications_api, notification_preferences, push_subscription, rfq_projects, rfq_requirements, daily_reports, contracts, site_inspections, material_inquiries, material_inquiries_enhanced, material_orders, e_signatures, etc. Variants include get_current_user_record (returns User ORM), get_current_user_optional, require_responder_role, require_vendor_role, require_designer_role. (2) get_current_user from app.core.auth — a stub returning hardcoded CurrentUser(user_id=1, username='demo_user'). Does NOT read headers or tokens. Used by smart_matching router. Additionally, routers/articles.py and routers/disputes.py use raw psycopg2 get_db_connection() with no auth dependency at all.

When create_transaction is called: (1) Amount converted to cents (int(amount_twd * 100)). (2) CommissionService.get_commission_type_from_transaction() determines type by checking: description contains 'premium' or payee_type='platform' with 'subscription' → 'premium_subscription'; material_order_id exists → 'material_order'; payee_type='designer' → 'design_fee'; payee_type='crew' → 'construction'; payee_type='vendor' → 'material_order'; payer_type='homeowner' with payee designer/platform → 'design_fee', crew → 'construction'; otherwise None. (3) If type found, calculate_commission() queries CommissionSetting for active setting (is_active=True, effective_from <= now, effective_to null or > now). Three possible outcomes: (a) 'no_setting' — no active setting → commission_amount=0, rate=0; (b) 'minimum' — calculated (amount × rate) below min_amount → set to min_amount; (c) 'calculated' — normal calculation; (d) 'maximum' — exceeds max_amount → capped. Fields populated: commission_type, commission_rate, commission_amount, platform_revenue.

In material_inquiries_enhanced.py: Trigger: when create_inquiry is called with auto_quote_enabled=True, background task try_auto_quote(inquiry_id, db) is scheduled via FastAPI BackgroundTasks. Trust score: before creating inquiry, SQL joins vendors → crews → crew_reviews to compute AVG(rating) as trust_score (default 3.0) and COUNT(rating) as review_count, stored on inquiry. Auto-quote price: try_auto_quote finds matching AutoQuoteRule (vendor_id, is_active=True, product_id matches or NULL, quantity in range). Gets latest base price from price_history (fallback 1200.0). Price = rule.calculate_price(base_price, quantity): if fixed_price set returns that, otherwise base_price × price_multiplier × quantity. Confidence based on trust: base 0.60; trust >= 4.0 → 0.95; >= 3.5 → 0.85; >= 3.0 → 0.75; below 3.0 → 0.60. Inquiry updated: status='auto_quoted', auto_quote_triggered=True, auto_quote_price, auto_quote_confidence, quoted_price=auto_price, quoted_at (now + auto_reply_delay_hours), delivery_estimate_days (7 if trust >= 4.0, else 10).

When a vendor revises a quote (submit_quote and revise_quote in rfq_chat_quotes.py): (1) Supersede: all existing 'pending' quotes in the same room set to status='superseded'. (2) Preserving confirmed items: before superseding, confirmed items (qi.confirmed == True) are collected from old quotes. These items are physically moved to the new quote by updating their quote_id to the new quote's ID and reassigning sort_order starting from 0. Confirmed items retain all original data. (3) Preventing duplicates: when iterating body.items (new items), any item whose name matches a confirmed item's name is skipped (if item.name in confirmed_names_from_old: continue). (4) New quote's total_amount includes both new items' totals AND carried-over confirmed items' subtotals. In revise_quote, previous_price is auto-populated from original quote's item prices via orig_price_by_name lookup.

Excluded entity type: 'materials'. Reason: materials' thumbnails come from product_images (managed by product-service), not uploaded through this endpoint. ENTITY_ALLOWED_TYPES only contains 'requirements', 'chat', 'projects'. Validation chain: (1) entity_type must be 'requirements'/'projects'/'chat' — else HTTP 400. (2) Entity ownership/permission: 'projects' → RfqProject exists and owner_id matches; 'requirements' → RfqRequirement exists and owner_id matches; 'chat' → RfqChatRoom exists and user is owner or responder — else HTTP 403. (3) File size ≤ MAX_FILE_SIZE (50 MB) — else HTTP 413. (4) MIME type: 'application/octet-stream' checks against ALLOWED_CAD_EXTENSIONS (.dwg, .dxf); otherwise checks ENTITY_ALLOWED_TYPES[entity_type] (images, PDF, video, CAD) — else HTTP 415. (5) Upload: RfqBlobClient uploads to temp-uploads first, copies to rfq-uploads/{entity_type}/{entity_id}/{uuid}.{ext}, deletes temp.

In create_requirement (rfq_requirements.py) with publish_type='direct' and vendor_ids: (1) RfqRequirement created with body fields + owner_id. (2) Batch query fetches Vendor records matching vendor_ids. (3) For each vendor: RfqRequirementResponder created with requirement_id, responder_id=vendor.user_id, is_designated=True. (4) For each vendor: get_or_create_chat_room() called with project_id, owner_id, responder_id, source_type='requirement', source_id=req.id. (5) System message RfqChatMessage created: '業主已指定您回應需求「{title}」'. (6) RfqRequirementResponder updated with chat_room_id and contacted_at. All within single db.commit(). Chat room uniqueness: get_or_create_chat_room() queries for existing active room matching (project_id + responder_id + owner_id + status='active'). If found, returns it. On concurrent INSERT IntegrityError, does db.rollback() and re-queries. Multiple materials/requirements targeting same vendor in same project share the same chat room.

Two database connection mechanisms: (1) SQLAlchemy ORM via app.core.database — uses create_engine() with connection pool (pool_size, max_overflow, pool_pre_ping=True). Provides get_db() dependency yielding Session objects. Used by the vast majority of API modules: all app/api/ files (rfq_chat, rfq_projects, rfq_requirements, daily_reports, contracts, inspections, inquiries, orders, e-signatures, notifications, push), all app/api/v1/ files (payments, insurance, warranty, review, disputes, sop, vendor_analytics), and most app/routers/ files (beta_testing, gallery, insurance, location, matching, onboarding, reviews, smart_matching, sop, warranty, commission, disputes). (2) Raw psycopg2 via app.database — uses psycopg2.connect() directly with individual connection params (DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD). No connection pooling. Used by only two modules: routers/articles.py and routers/disputes.py. They coexist because articles and disputes routers were written with raw SQL (no ORM models) using direct psycopg2 connections, while the rest of the service standardized on SQLAlchemy ORM.

Daily report status constraints and auto-populated fields: On submission (POST /daily-reports): No explicit status constraint — creates with default status='draft' from model definition. System auto-populates: submitted_by (set to authenticated user's id), created_at (server_default=func.now()), updated_at (server_default=func.now()). On update (PATCH /daily-reports/{id}): Status must be 'draft' — if report.status != 'draft', raises HTTP 400 '僅草稿狀態可編輯'. System auto-populates: updated_at = func.now(). On approval (PATCH /daily-reports/{id}/approve): Status must NOT be 'approved' — if report.status == 'approved', raises HTTP 400 '日報已核准'. System auto-populates: status set to 'approved', approved_by set to authenticated user's id, approved_at = func.now(), updated_at = func.now().

When a vendor's summary stats are updated via upsert_vendor_summary(), the method first upserts the item into Cosmos DB's vendor_summaries container, then calls await self.cache.delete(vendor_id) to invalidate the Redis cache. Two layers involved: (1) Cosmos DB (data layer) — source-of-truth document upserted via container.upsert_item(item). (2) Redis (cache layer) — cached entry deleted via analytics_cache.delete(vendor_id), which constructs key as 'analytics:vendor_summary:{vendor_id}' and calls redis_client.delete(cache_key). Next read will miss cache, fetch fresh data from Cosmos DB, and re-cache with TTL (default 300 seconds / 5 minutes).

Two entity types: vendors and designers, with separate AnalyticsCache instances differentiated by CACHE_PREFIX: analytics_cache uses 'analytics:vendor_summary:' (default), designer_analytics_cache uses 'analytics:designer_summary:' (passed via prefix parameter). Both are global instances created at module level. If wrong cache instance used (e.g., analytics_cache for designer): key would be 'analytics:vendor_summary:{designer_id}' instead of 'analytics:designer_summary:{designer_id}'. Consequences: (1) cache misses when correct instance reads, (2) potential data collision if vendor and designer share same numeric ID — serving wrong stats, (3) cache invalidation on upsert deletes wrong key, leaving stale data.

To add favorites to last 30 days: (1) Schema StatsDetailLast30d in models/stats_schemas.py — add favorites: int = 0 (currently only has profile_views, product_views, catalog_views, contact_clicks). (2) Service _get_default_stats() in stats_service.py — add 'favorites': 0 to the last_30_days dict. (3) The cronjob (outside this service) that computes and upserts last_30d must calculate favorites for the last 30 days and include it. (4) The upsert_vendor_summary() callers must include favorites in the last_30d dict. Note: get_vendor_stats() reads from Cosmos DB using .get() so it passes through fields automatically if schemas include them.

Detection: the code checks if ':10000' in self.redis_url. When Azure Managed Redis detected: uses RedisCluster (from redis.asyncio.cluster), parses URL via urlparse(), connects with explicit host, port (default 10000), password, ssl=True, ssl_cert_reqs='none', ssl_check_hostname=False, decode_responses=False, socket_connect_timeout=10, socket_timeout=10. Standard Redis: uses aredis.from_url(self.redis_url) with only socket_timeout=10 and socket_connect_timeout=10 — no explicit SSL or cluster mode.

Input: comma-separated string via query parameter product_ids (e.g., ?product_ids=1,2,3). Validation: (1) each segment stripped and parsed as int() — non-integer raises ValueError caught as HTTP 400; (2) empty list returns HTTP 400; (3) max 100 IDs enforced with HTTP 400. Query: builds Cosmos DB query with f-string: id_list = ', '.join([f"'{pid}'" for pid in product_ids]) then f"SELECT ... WHERE c.id IN ({id_list})", uses enable_cross_partition_query=True. SQL injection risk: product_ids are converted to int first (sanitizes), so direct injection blocked. However, uses string interpolation (f-string) rather than parameterized @parameter syntax. If int() validation were bypassed/removed, this would be a direct injection vector.

Normalization: days = 7 if days <= 7 else 30. For days=15 (not ≤ 7), result is 30. FastAPI Query enforces ge=7, le=30, so valid inputs 7-30, but 8-30 all become 30, only 7 stays 7. For dates with no data: _build_timeline() iterates start_date to end_date day by day, looks up date_str in items_dict. Missing dates return {} via .get(date_str, {}), each metric defaults to 0 via .get('profile_views', 0) etc. Timeline always has contiguous days with zero-filled gaps.

The mock's query_items() ignores query string and parameters entirely. It filters self._data.values() by item.get('vendor_id') == partition_key. Differences from real Cosmos DB: (1) no SQL parsing — date range filters ignored, ALL items for vendor_id returned. (2) No ORDER BY. (3) Hardcodes vendor_id check — testing designer timelines (filtering on designer_id) returns nothing. (4) No cross-partition query support — product export stats uses enable_cross_partition_query=True with no partition_key, but mock requires it. Impact on vendor timeline testing: tests receive all daily stats regardless of date range, making 7-day vs 30-day filtering unverifiable. Timeline builder still fills zeros but items_dict contains extra out-of-range data.

Health check (GET /health) checks ONLY Redis — calls analytics_cache.health_check() which does redis_client.ping(). NOT checked: (1) Cosmos DB (primary analytics data store), (2) PostgreSQL. If Cosmos DB goes down, health check would NOT detect it — still reports healthy as long as Redis responds. The overall status is hardcoded to 'healthy' regardless of Redis state.

The top portfolios endpoint manually constructs PortfolioViewStats objects from raw dicts using .get() with defaults: portfolio_id=p.get('portfolio_id', 0), title=p.get('title', ''), cover_image_url=p.get('cover_image_url', ''), view_count=p.get('view_count', 0). Response wrapped as {'portfolios': [...]}. Other endpoints return service data more directly. If data store returns items missing 'title' or 'cover_image_url', .get() provides safe defaults: empty strings for title and cover_image_url, 0 for view_count and portfolio_id. No error raised — gracefully returns portfolios with empty/zero fields, unlike direct dict access (p['title']) which would raise KeyError.
